title: Flow field
sub: Thousands of units, one goal: the cost field, the integration field and the direction field, a comparison with A* per agent, rebuilding and Jobs
cards/0/title: A thousand units and one goal
cards/0/body:
A strategy game: the player selects 500 units and clicks a point. Tower defense: hundreds of creeps walk from the spawn to the exit. A zombie horde runs at the player. Everyone has one goal, and A* per unit means 500 searches, each covering much of the same ground.

A flow field turns the problem around: one search from the goal across the whole map, and then each unit reads the arrow in its own cell — O(1) per unit per frame. Three layers:

1. The cost field — the cost of entering a cell: 1 is flat ground, up to 9 is mud or water, 0 is a wall (games often use a byte of 1–255, with 255 as the wall).
2. The integration field — what it costs to get from a cell to the nearest goal. This is Dijkstra from all goals at once; with uniform cell costs it is the same multi-source BFS as in 01 Matrix (#542) from the unit on graphs.
3. The direction field — in every cell, an arrow to the neighbour with the smallest integration.
cards/1/q: A 128 × 128 map (16,384 cells), 1000 units, all with the same goal. Which is cheaper?
cards/1/options/0: One field: Dijkstra at ≈ 3·10⁵ operations for everyone, and one arrow read per unit
cards/1/options/1: A* per unit: the paths are short, so in total it beats one field over the whole map
cards/1/options/2: The same: both are O(number of cells)
cards/1/explain: The field is one Dijkstra over 16,384 cells: about 16,384 · (14 + 4) ≈ 3·10⁵ operations and 80 KB of memory (an int of integration and an sbyte arrow per cell), shared by all. A*, even at 1000 expanded cells per unit, is 10⁶ heap operations in total plus 1000 paths in memory — and the same again every time the goal moves and paths are rebuilt.
cards/1/wrong/1: A short path does not mean a cheap search: A* expands cells around the path, and for 1000 units that is 1000 nearly identical searches.
cards/1/wrong/2: O(cells) is one field for everyone. A* is O(cells) per unit in the worst case — 1000 times more.
cards/2/title: The integration field: Dijkstra from the goals
cards/2/body:
Every goal gets 0 and goes into the heap at once — like all the zeros in 01 Matrix: the wave spreads from all goals together, and every cell learns its cost to the nearest one. A neighbour gets d + cost[neighbour]: the cost sits on the cell being entered.

A subtlety interviewers like: here "the first touch is final" is correct, even though in the Dijkstra lesson it was a bug. All neighbours of a cell v offer it d_u + cost[v] with the same cost[v], and the neighbours leave the heap in increasing d_u. So whoever touches v first has offered the minimum. Each cell enters the heap once — there are no stale entries, and the heap never exceeds the number of cells.

Walls (cost 0) are never entered; cells cut off by walls stay at ∞. Time is O(V log V), where V is the number of cells.
cards/3/q: Assemble both phases: integration and directions.
cards/3/explain: Skip a wall (cost 0). Leave alone a cell that already has an integration value: the first touch is final because the cost sits on the cell itself. The neighbour gets d plus the cost of entering it, not of the current cell. The arrow points at the neighbour with the smallest integration — the remaining cost to the goal; walls and cut-off cells hold ∞ there and are never chosen.
cards/4/task: Step through building the field on a 5 × 7 map with the goal G at (2, 6). The large number in a cell is its integration, the small one in the corner is the cost of the cell. The rig asks twice: what is written into a mud cell, and what happens to a cell cut off by walls.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Nothing: wait for (2, 2) first — it might be cheaper through there
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: 28 = 10 + 9 + 9: the cost of its own cell and the neighbour's
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: (2, 4) leaves the heap with integration 10. Its neighbour (2, 3) is mud costing 9 and is still at ∞. On the other side (2, 3) borders (2, 2) with integration 12, which is still in the heap. What is written into (2, 3)?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: A neighbour gets d + cost[neighbour] = 10 + 9 = 19. (2, 2) comes out later — 12 ≥ 10 — and would offer 12 + 9 = 21: the cost of entering (2, 3) is the same, and d is larger. That is why the first touch is final, and the "already has a value" check loses nothing.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: No arrow: −1, a unit there cannot reach the goal
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: An arrow to the neighbour with the smallest integration, like everyone else
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: The integration is done and phase 3 begins. In row 0, cell (0, 6) is still at ∞: there is a wall (0, 5) to its left and a wall (1, 6) below. What does it get in the direction field?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: The direction loop skips cells with integration ∞ (and the goal itself, at 0): Direction stays −1. The game has to handle that — a unit in such a cell stands still or picks another goal — rather than marching it into a wall.
cards/5/q: On this field some units walk into walls, and the rest wander without getting closer to the goal. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: The arrow picks a neighbour by its entry cost, and that cost is local: it knows nothing about where the goal is. Worse, a wall costs 0 — less than anything — so arrows point straight into walls. What is needed is the integration, the remaining cost to the goal: int v = Integration[y * cols + x]. Walls and cut-off cells hold ∞ there and are never chosen.
cards/6/title: Unity: units on the field, and Jobs
cards/6/body:
Movement. Arrows in 4 directions give a staircase path. The fixes: 8 directions; a direction from the difference of the neighbours' integration, like a gradient, interpolated inside the cell; and "line of sight" — if there are no walls between the unit and the goal, it walks straight.

Crowds. The field does not stop units from piling onto each other: everyone in a cell gets the same arrow. You need local avoidance — separation from the nearest neighbours, and the spatial grid from the next lesson finds those neighbours cheaply.

Memory. 16,384 cells is 64 KB of integration in int and 16 KB of arrows in sbyte. The arrays live in fields and are not reallocated on every rebuild.

Jobs and Burst. Dijkstra is sequential — one heap — so integration runs as one IJob per goal. The direction field, though, is fully parallel: a cell's arrow depends only on its neighbours' integration, so it is an IJobParallelFor over cells.
cards/7/q: Where does a flow field beat A* per agent? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/0: Tower defense: hundreds of creeps walk from the spawn to a single exit
cards/7/options/1: Strategy: the player selected 200 units and clicked one point
cards/7/options/2: A zombie horde runs at the player; the field is rebuilt when the player changes cells
cards/7/options/3: Five heroes, each with a quest in a different corner of the map
cards/7/options/4: One unit on a 4096 × 4096 map heading for a goal 20 cells away
cards/7/explain: A field pays off when the goal is shared: one rebuild serves everyone. Five different goals means five fields over the whole map against five short A* searches. One unit and a nearby goal means a field of 1.7·10⁷ cells for a 20-step path, where A* expands a few dozen cells.
cards/8/title: The map changes: rebuilding the field
cards/8/body:
When to rebuild. The field depends on the map and on the goals. In tower defense the player places a tower, and a cell becomes a wall. In a chase the goal — the player — moves. Rebuild on events: a tower was placed, the player moved into another cell — not every frame. A full rebuild of 128 × 128 is about 3·10⁵ operations, a fraction of a millisecond.

The classic TD question: how do you stop the player from walling off the path? Before placing a tower, build the field with the tower as a wall and check that the spawn's integration is not ∞. If it is ∞, refuse and restore the field without the tower.

Partial updates. If a cell got cheaper or a wall was knocked down, integration can only decrease — it is enough to push the changed cell with its new value and continue Dijkstra from it, with the condition "got smaller" rather than "not touched yet": the wave reaches exactly the cells that improved. If a cell got more expensive or a wall appeared, everyone whose path ran through it may get worse; they have to be found and reset. On small maps a full rebuild is simpler.
cards/8/deep:
Hierarchy by chunks. On a 1024 × 1024 map one field is 10⁶ cells, and rebuilding it on every click is expensive. The map is split into sectors, say 16 × 16, with portals — openings on their borders. First A* over the small portal graph picks the sectors to pass through, then fields are built only for those sectors, portal to portal, and cached per "sector, goal" pair. It is the same trick as HPA* for A*.

Why Dijkstra and not BFS. With uniform cell costs the integration field is a multi-source BFS, O(V) with no heap. Costs of 1–9 call for the bucket queue from the Dijkstra lesson: the weights are small integers, and buckets by integration value avoid the log.

Parallel integration. Dijkstra cannot be parallelised, but integration can be computed by iteration: each IJobParallelFor pass sets a cell to the minimum over its neighbours, until nothing changes. It takes as many passes as the longest path is long — hundreds on an open map — so it only pays off on many cores with Burst. Smoother arrows come from solving the eikonal equation (fast marching): integration in a "continuous" metric, without Manhattan diamonds.

Compactness. Cost as a byte, integration as a ushort up to 65,535, an arrow in 3 bits for 8 directions. A 256 × 256 field is about 320 KB in int and sbyte and about 160 KB in compact form: half the memory, and half the data every unit and every rebuild has to read.
cards/9/q: Tower defense: the player places towers, and creeps follow a flow field. How do you stop the player from walling off the path from the spawn to the exit?
cards/9/options/0: Before placing, build the field with the tower as a wall and check the spawn's integration is not ∞
cards/9/options/1: Forbid placing a tower right next to another tower
cards/9/options/2: After placing, run A* from every creep and remove the tower if any of them fails
cards/9/explain: The spawn's integration is exactly the answer to "can you get from the spawn to the exit". One rebuild before placing, and the decision is made before any creep notices anything.
cards/9/wrong/1: An adjacency rule does not check connectivity: in a one-cell-wide corridor a single tower with no neighbours blocks the path, while towers side by side in the open are often perfectly safe.
cards/9/wrong/2: A* from every creep is hundreds of searches instead of one field, and only after the tower is already up. The check belongs before placement.
cards/10/q: You are asked how to move 1000 units to one point. Put the steps of your answer in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: one goal or several, how often the map and the goal change, 4 or 8 directions
cards/10/items/1: Baseline: A* per unit — 1000 nearly identical searches, estimate their cost
cards/10/items/2: Idea: one search from the goal — Dijkstra over the whole map starting from all goals
cards/10/items/3: Three fields: cost, integration, directions; a unit reads its cell's arrow in O(1)
cards/10/items/4: Why the first touch is final: the cost sits on the cell being entered
cards/10/items/5: Cost: O(V log V) per rebuild, O(1) per unit, memory for two arrays of V
cards/10/items/6: A real game: rebuild on events, cut-off cells, crowds and Jobs
cards/10/explain: Start by asking whether there is one goal: that decides whether a field wins at all. Then an honest baseline with A* and its cost, the idea and the three layers. The senior part is why the first touch is right here, what it costs, and what to do with a changing map and a crowd.
cards/11/q: Match each layer or technique with what it gives you.
cards/11/pairs/0/1: The cost of entering a cell, 0 is a wall
cards/11/pairs/1/1: The cost of the path to the nearest goal
cards/11/pairs/2/1: An arrow to the neighbour with less integration
cards/11/pairs/3/0: All goals in the heap at once
cards/11/pairs/3/1: Every cell leads to its nearest goal
cards/11/pairs/4/1: A tower cut the path — refuse
